source.title: Spec-Driven Development in Scrum and Kanban: Where the Spec Actually Lives
source.author: Jaroslaw Wasowski

sections.title: Where the spec lives in the cycle
When it works and when it fails

theses.label: Agents don't ask
theses.text: An AI agent builds exactly what the contract says: where a human would ask a follow-up question, it builds the wrong thing with full confidence.
theses.note: The article's opening contrast: the same team runs one sprint from a story and a conversation, and another from a contract that an agent implements.

theses.label: Spec quality is output quality
theses.text: With an agent in the repository, the quality of the spec becomes the quality of the output.
theses.note: A vague prompt turns the sprint into a string of fixes.

theses.label: Frozen or living spec
theses.text: A spec can be frozen, agreed up front and defended against change by phase gates, or living, maturing inside the sprint as the implementation teaches the team.
theses.note: The frozen variant is Big Design Up Front, and it is what gives SDD its bad name.

theses.label: Agile never banned docs
theses.text: The Agile Manifesto ranks working software above comprehensive documentation without excluding documentation.
theses.note: Its authors added that there is value on the right side too.

theses.label: Agility is the right to change
theses.text: Agility isn't the absence of a contract but the contract's right to change after the build starts.
theses.note: The article quotes Eisenhower: "Plans are worthless, but planning is everything."

theses.label: The tension: frozen vs living
theses.text: The real tension is between a frozen spec and a living one, not between fast delivery and writing specs: only a frozen spec deserves the waterfall charge.
theses.note: So the common objection that SDD is waterfall in Markdown targets the spec's presence instead of its being frozen.

theses.label: AI sped up greenfield work
theses.text: A controlled study on a greenfield task showed a clear speedup with an AI assistant.

theses.label: AI slowed legacy work
theses.text: A study on a mature repository with millions of lines of code showed a slowdown for experienced developers.
theses.note: Different conditions, different results: the author reads the two studies as two ends of the same axis.

theses.label: Gaps become wrong code
theses.text: On mature code, gaps a human would question turn into wrong implementations.

theses.label: The spec closes the gaps
theses.text: The spec is the place to close those gaps, before the agent starts building.

theses.label: Three levels of spec
theses.text: SDD comes in three levels: spec-first, where the spec leads but the code is what's maintained; spec-anchored, where the spec is versioned and evolves with the code; and spec-as-source, where the spec is the source of truth and the code is generated.
theses.note: The classification is by Birgitta Böckeler of Thoughtworks.

theses.label: Higher levels cost more
theses.text: Each higher level raises the maintenance cost and the coupling between spec and code.

theses.label: When a higher level pays
theses.text: A higher level pays off only where its cost buys something: spec-anchored where several teams or agents share one contract, and spec-as-source in experiments or where certification requires a formal model anyway.

theses.label: "Spec" is a blurry word
theses.text: "Spec" can mean anything from an elaborate prompt to dozens of Markdown files.

theses.label: A statistic needs its level
theses.text: An SDD statistic means nothing without the level of spec it was measured at.
theses.note: A metric from a spec-anchored project doesn't transfer to a simple bug fix; the author calls conflating levels the costliest mistake in the whole topic.

theses.label: Pick the lowest level that fits
theses.text: Each piece of work should get the lowest level of spec that fits it, not the level another project's numbers favor: spec-first for most work, spec-anchored for contracts shared across teams, and spec-as-source only for experiments and safety-critical systems.
theses.note: The one antipattern is paying for a higher level while the problem sits on a lower one, such as a simple bug that spawns several stories and a dozen acceptance criteria.

theses.label: The spec lives in the sprint
theses.text: The backlog should stay at the level of goal and intent, and the contract should be developed inside the sprint, as part of doing the work.
theses.note: The author credits Yuval Yeret with this placement. A finished contract in the backlog signals a spec at the wrong level of abstraction.

theses.label: The spec feeds the DoR
theses.text: A spec already supplies what a Definition of Ready asks for: acceptance criteria, scope boundaries and edge cases.

theses.label: A DoR can become a gate
theses.text: A Definition of Ready can turn into a gatekeeper that blocks the iteration and drifts back toward waterfall.
theses.note: This is Mike Cohn's warning, quoted in the article.

theses.label: Scrum: DoR as agreement
theses.text: In Scrum the spec belongs in the Definition of Ready, treated as the team's agreement on entry quality rather than a phase gate.

theses.label: Kanban: the commitment point
theses.text: In Kanban the commitment point takes the role of the Definition of Ready: a task crosses it only once it's ready to pull.
theses.note: Before that point lives Upstream Kanban, the analysis and contract design ahead of the main flow, with WIP limits that keep specs from going stale before anyone builds them.

theses.label: A spec sped up Scrum
theses.text: In a quasi-experiment, Scrum with an architectural spec raised velocity by about 19% and cut defect density by about 31%.
theses.note: sMBSAP, Colorado State, 2023. The author notes it's a single project: a direction, not a guarantee.

theses.label: A full spec halved defects
theses.text: A semiconductor product line had about half the defects after the team introduced a full, reviewed spec, despite higher complexity.

theses.label: BDD specs cut firefighting
theses.text: At a global bank, firefighting dropped from over a third of developer time to single digits after nine months of behavior-driven specs.

theses.label: Those specs fitted
theses.text: In those three cases the spec matched the scale of the problem.

theses.label: Fitted specs paid off
theses.text: Where the spec matches the scale of the problem, quality goes up.

theses.label: Rigid SDD slowed a CRUD
theses.text: A rigid SDD workflow on a small CRUD feature slowed a practitioner down roughly tenfold.
theses.note: The tool generated more Markdown than code, and all of it had to be reviewed: spec drift in its early stage.

theses.label: A mandate backfired
theses.text: SDD imposed top-down as a mandate turned the organization against it.
theses.note: A petition of more than a thousand engineers, with metric-gaming in the background; the author notes that some details are unverified.

theses.label: Fit decides, not presence
theses.text: What decides the outcome is fitting the spec level to the context, not the mere presence of a spec.

theses.label: Perception isn't measurement
theses.text: Developers who expected AI to speed them up by about 24% were measured to be about 19% slower on a mature repository.
theses.note: METR, 2025: sixteen developers, wide confidence interval. The author calls the gap between perception and metrics the real opponent.

theses.label: Roll it out as an experiment
theses.text: SDD should be rolled out as an experiment that tracks cycle time, rework rate and the ratio of code to Markdown, not imposed as a mandate.

theses.label: Shrink the batch
theses.text: When rework or spec files grow faster than code, the batch size should shrink, not the process grow.

theses.label: One owner, a version history
theses.text: A living spec needs a single owner and a version history, or spec drift comes back.
theses.note: The author also caps invariant rules: too many fixed constraints don't add order; they add places for contradictions to hide.

theses.label: Living, fitted, measured
theses.text: SDD strengthens Agile when the spec is living: developed inside the sprint, or before the commitment point in Kanban, as an agreement rather than a gate, at the level the problem needs, and judged by measurement rather than by feel.
theses.note: The article's answer to its opening question: the faster sprint was the one where the spec lived inside the sprint at the right level.

issues.explanation: The mandate failure shows another deciding factor, how SDD was introduced, so it can't show that fitting the level is what decides the outcome.
issues.quote: Still, the conclusion is clear: what decides the outcome is fitting the level to the context, not the mere presence of a spec.

issues.explanation: The article never says which level of spec the three success cases used: the fit is read off the good outcome. By the article's own rule (15), a statistic without its level means nothing.
issues.quote: Three different contexts, one direction: when the spec matched the scale of the problem, quality went up.

issues.explanation: SDD is defined as an AI agent building from a contract, but none of the three success cases involves an agent: they show that specs helped, not that SDD with agents does.
issues.quote: In a quasi-experiment comparing Scrum with a version enriched by an architectural spec (sMBSAP, Colorado State, 2023)

issues.explanation: "Level" is a rung of the ladder in 11, 16 and 29, but a level of abstraction (goal or finished contract) in 17; the sentence treats a finished contract in the backlog as a lower rung.
issues.quote: Placing a finished, complete contract in the backlog is a signal that the spec sits at the wrong level of abstraction, one rung too low relative to the intent.

issues.explanation: A Definition of Ready is what a task must meet before it enters the sprint, yet 17 develops the contract only after the task is pulled in. Both hold only if the DoR checks a partial spec, which the article doesn't say; Kanban's commitment point (21) has the same tension.
issues.quote: The spec already supplies what the DoR requires: acceptance criteria, scope boundaries, and edge cases.

issues.explanation: The opening compares a sprint that starts from a story with one that starts from a contract; the summary answers by comparing a living contract with a frozen one, a pair the opening never set up.
issues.quote: The one that delivered faster was the one where the spec lived inside the sprint at the right level — not the one that got a finished, frozen contract handed down from the backlog.

issues.explanation: The batch-size rule follows only if rework or spec files growing faster than code show that the spec has outgrown the problem. The article doesn't say so, and the remedy that fit (29) suggests would be a lower level, not a smaller batch.
issues.quote: If the share of rework grows after the rollout, or the number of spec files bloats faster than the code, that’s a signal to pull back the batch size, not to pile on more process.

senses.definition: A precise contract written before the code, from which an AI agent builds the implementation.
Any practice that writes a spec before the code, with or without an agent.
A rung of Böckeler's ladder: spec-first, spec-anchored or spec-as-source.
A level of abstraction: goal and intent, or a finished contract.
A contract that matures inside the sprint as the implementation teaches the team.
A design agreed up front and defended against change by phase gates.
The criteria a task must meet before it enters the sprint.
In Kanban, the moment a task stops being optional and becomes a commitment to deliver.
The gap between the spec and the code once there are more documents than the team can maintain.

Defines the two kinds of spec the article compares.
Checkable in the Manifesto itself, whose authors say there is value in the items on the right.
Restates the Manifesto's own value: responding to change over following a plan.
An unnamed controlled study; the article gives neither its source nor its numbers.

condition.text: Nothing but gaps no one questioned explains the slowdown on mature code.
condition.reason: questionable cause: the study doesn't say why the developers were slower

condition.text: Closing the gaps in the spec, before the agent builds, is the best way to avoid wrong implementations.
condition.reason: the alternatives, such as an agent that asks back, aren't considered

reconstructed.reason: Birgitta Böckeler's classification, named and checkable.
Follows from the definitions: each higher level keeps more of the spec in step with the code.
Common practice: shared API contracts are versioned and tested, and certification asks for formal models.
Common knowledge; the tools the article mentions range from a prompt to many Markdown files.

condition.text: No other choice of level weighs cost against payoff better.
condition.reason: each level's cost is weighed against where it pays off

condition.text: Developing the contract inside the sprint is the best way to keep the spec living.
condition.reason: the alternative, a finished contract in the backlog, is shown to freeze it

reconstructed.reason: Common knowledge: acceptance criteria, scope boundaries and edge cases are what both contain.
Mike Cohn's warning, quoted; he writes on this exact point.

condition.text: Treating the DoR as an agreement is the best way to use the spec without a gate.
Kanban's commitment point is like Scrum's DoR in the respect that matters: it's where a task must be ready to build.
condition.reason: the article states the shared role: a task crosses it only when it's ready to pull

reconstructed.reason: A single project, as the author notes: it points to a direction, not a guarantee.
A single, unnamed product line.

condition.text: The three cases are enough and representative.
condition.reason: three successes picked for one direction

condition.text: Nothing but the fit of the spec level explains why some rollouts paid off and others failed.
condition.reason: the fit is judged after the fact, and other differences between the cases aren't ruled out

reconstructed.reason: A named, checkable study (METR, 2025), with its limits stated: sixteen developers, wide confidence interval.

condition.text: An experiment with tracked metrics is the best way to roll out SDD.
condition.reason: the measured gap between perception and speed calls for metrics, and the alternative, a mandate, failed

reconstructed.label: Bloat means the spec outgrew

reconstructed.reason: Backed only by the CRUD case (27), where Markdown outgrew code on a small feature.
